`tail`: output the last part of files.

## Synopsis

<strong>tail</strong> \[<strong>-f</strong>\] \[<strong>-n</strong> \[<em>+</em>\]<em>lines</em>\] \[<strong>-c</strong> \[<em>+</em>\]<em>bytes</em>\] \[<em>file</em>...\]

## Description

<strong>tail</strong> writes the last 10 lines of each <em>file</em> to standard output. With no file, or for a file named <strong>-</strong>, it reads standard input. With more than one file, each is headed by <strong>==\></strong> <em>name</em> <strong>\<==</strong> (standard input is named <strong>standard input</strong>), with a blank line before every heading but the first.

## Options

<strong>-f</strong>
: Follows: once the files are shown, waits, and shows what is added to them, until it's stopped (^C, or <strong>kill</strong>). Everything is shown the moment it comes: files on a disk or in <strong>/tmp</strong> are watched (inotify: a disk reports each change made on it), and pipes and device files are waited on with <strong>poll</strong>, all together. A file rewritten rather than added to (a disk file grown shorter, or a device whose state changed, as a redstone card's) is shown again from its start, after <strong>tail:</strong> <em>file</em><strong>: file truncated</strong> on standard error. A heading names the file when the text is another file's than the last shown. Standard input isn't followed. A device file is read only as far as it has something now, so one that never ends (a motion sensor's: an event a line) shows the last of the events waiting, then each as it comes.

<strong>-n</strong> <em>lines</em>
: The last <em>lines</em> lines. +<em>lines</em> starts at line <em>lines</em> instead (1 is the first), and goes on to the end.

<strong>-c</strong> <em>bytes</em>
: The last <em>bytes</em> bytes; +<em>bytes</em> starts at that byte and goes on to the end.

<strong>-</strong><em>number</em>
: The same as <strong>-n</strong> <em>number</em>.

The number may be joined to its option (<strong>-n5</strong>) or follow it as the next argument. A later <strong>-n</strong> undoes an earlier <strong>-c</strong>.

## Exit status

0 on success; 1 if a number or an option is invalid, or a file can't be opened (the other files are still shown).

## Examples

```text
tail -n 3 /init.lua
tail -n +2 list.txt
ps | tail -c 100
tail -f /dev/redstone0
tail -f /dev/motion0
```

## Notes

What another program writes to a file on a disk shows when it closes the file (a disk's files take writes at close), so <strong>tail -f</strong> sees a line once its writer has closed the file; <strong>\>\></strong> in the shell closes it at once. GNU <strong>tail</strong> reads a device's file to its end first, so on one that never ends (a sensor's events) it shows nothing; with <strong>-f</strong>, this one reads only what the device has now, then follows it. A change made to a disk's file outside the computer (on the disk's host) isn't seen until the next change made inside it.

## See also

<strong>head</strong>(1), <strong>cat</strong>(1), <strong>grep</strong>(1)
